title: Near itinerancy and slow singlet formation in the triangular lattice NaRuO2
authors: Charles C. Tam, Alon Hendler Avidor, Pritam Bhattacharyya, Yongseong Choi, Daniel Haskel, Sven Luther, Hlynur Gretarrson, Liviu Hozoi, Stephen D. Wilson
abstract: NaRuO$_2$ forms a delafossite-like structure that contains triangular sublattices of edge-sharing RuO$_6$ octahedra. It shows no evidence of magnetic order down to 100 mK and persistent spin fluctuations, suggestive of a quantum disordered magnetic ground state. In order to characterize the physical regime from which this disordered state arises, we use resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) and X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) at the Ru-$L_{2,3}$-edge, along with pulsed high-field magnetization to characterize both the local electronic structure and the magnetic interactions. Despite significant spin-orbit coupling inferred from XAS measurements, a spin-orbit exciton, characteristic of a spin-orbit assisted Mott insulator, was not observed with RIXS due to the presence of damped intraorbital excitations, which are characteristic of a metal. Corroborated by models of the high-field magnetization to a random singlet model, we propose a picture of a nearly itinerant system with strong magnetic and charge fluctuations that destabilize long-range magnetic order.
summary: This work investigates the exotic magnetic state of NaRuO2, finding that its behavior is best described as a nearly itinerant system rather than a simple Mott insulator. By combining RIXS and high-field magnetization measurements with Random Singlet Model fitting, the authors conclude that strong charge fluctuations are key in suppressing long-range magnetic order into a slow singlet formation regime.
main_problem: To characterize the physical regime responsible for the quantum disordered magnetic ground state observed in NaRuO2, specifically distinguishing between contributions from charge fluctuations versus strong magnetic interactions.
main_result: The evidence points towards a nearly itinerant system dominated by strong magnetic and charge fluctuations that destabilize long-range magnetic order, suggesting slow singlet formation rather than purely localized magnetism.
method: A combination of advanced experimental techniques (RIXS, XAS, high-field magnetization) and theoretical modeling using the Random Singlet Model was employed.
model_or_system: The study focuses on NaRuO2, a ruthenate oxide with a triangular lattice structure exhibiting no magnetic order down to very low temperatures. The physics is analyzed through comparisons to Mott insulators and models like the Kitaev exchange model.
key_observables: XAS Branching Ratio (SOC strength), RIXS excitations (damped intraorbital modes), high-field magnetization scaling exponents ($\alpha$), and susceptibility temperature dependence ($\chi(T)$).
important_parameters: Low temperatures ($<100 	ext{ mK}$), SOC strength comparable to $\alpha$-RuCl3, and the power-law exponent $\alpha$ from RSS fits.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that deviations from simple magnetic ordering are governed by itinerant behavior and disorder effects, leading to a random singlet state description.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate XAS spectra comparing NaRuO2 to other materials, RIXS energy maps showing excitation modes (A, B, C), and magnetization data fitted to the Random Singlet State model.
paper_structure: The paper systematically uses spectroscopic measurements (XAS/RIXS) to probe electronic structure and then applies high-field magnetization and susceptibility analysis, fitting the results to the Random Singlet Model to deduce the nature of the magnetic ground state.
why_interesting: The interplay between charge fluctuations (suggested by RIXS findings) and magnetic disorder (confirmed by RSS fits) provides a rich model for understanding quantum criticality in strongly correlated oxides, relevant to many-body dynamics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Possible defect modes in the triangular lattice of NaRuO2. (a) Drawing of the unit cell of pristine NaRuO2. RuO6 and NaO6 octahedra have been drawn. (b) Illustration of a Na-Ru site mixing defect in NaRuO2. (c) Illustration of disordered honeycomb Na2RuO3, which is equivalent to NaRuO2 with a 1/3 occupation of Na on the Ru site.

FIG. 2. Branching ratios determined from Ru-L XAS. (a) XAS taken across the Ru L3 and L2 edges, on Ru and NaRuO2. Data are fit to an arctangent step function and Lorentzian, defined in the methods. (b) Experimenmtal branching ratio (BR), defined as the fit intensity at L3 divided by the intensity at L2 for Ru, NaRuO2, and α-RuCl3. The experimental BR for α-RuCl3 is taken from Ref. 11. Details on the BR calculation for NaRuO2 and α-RuCl3 are given in the methods.

FIG. 3. Ru-L3-edge resonant inelastic X-ray scatter- ing on polycrystalline NaRuO2. (a) XAS over the Ru L3 edge, taken in fluorescence yield at room temperature. Marked peaks correspond to excitations into t2g and eg states. Normalization and self-absorption corrections have not been applied due to the small energy range collected. (b) RIXS energy map over the L3 edge, showing three main features labelled A, B and C. RIXS data is momentum-averaged as the sample is polycrystalline, and taken at 20 K. (c) RIXS spectra at different incident energy slices showing their fits. (d) RIXS spectra normalized to intensity at 500 meV, where mode A is peaked.

FIG. 4. Low energy excitations in NaRuO2. (a) Fitted quasielastic RIXS intensity, as a function of incident energy. (b) RIXS response, taken at 2837 eV, where the datapoints are in red, fit is a red line, and quasielastic and phonon fit components are in blue and yellow. In green is the Q inte- grated energy cut inelastic neutron scattering data, taken at 1.8 K. The integration window is [0, 2] ˚A −1. Neutron data is from Ref. 26.

FIG. 5. Random singlet fits to magnetic measurements of NaRuO2. Fits of the random singlet model to (a) magneti- zation taken at T = 0.48 K up to 45 T, and (b) magnetic susceptibility at H = 0.1 T. Definitions of MRS(H) and χRS(T) are given in the main text. (c)-(f) RSS fits to high-field magnetization at various temperatures on a log-log scale.
